turns_text: [SEG0001] person_1 (DOCTOR): Sorry, the screen's just frozen on me. Give me a second. Right, what's been going on?

[SEG0002] person_2 (PATIENT): I've been completely exhausted, that's the main thing, and I'm getting breathless, and my periods have been horrendous for about a year. I keep thinking I'll bounce back and I just don't.
[SEG0003] person_3 (FAMILY_MEMBER): I'm her sister, Claire. She's not herself. She nods off by half seven.
[SEG0004] person_1 (DOCTOR): Exhausted and breathless. How long for the tiredness, sorry, say it again, I was clicking the wrong tab.

[SEG0005] person_2 (PATIENT): The periods have been heavy for about a year. The tiredness I noticed properly after Easter, so a few months, but I reckon it started with the periods, I just blamed the library being short-staffed.
[SEG0006] person_1 (DOCTOR): Breathless when you're moving about, or at rest as well?

[SEG0007] person_2 (PATIENT): When I'm moving. The stairs up to the flat finish me off, I have to stop halfway and wait, and if I've got the shopping it's worse. I'm not gasping sitting here, though. I do the returns desk and the children's section, lots of bending.
[SEG0008] person_3 (FAMILY_MEMBER): She sat on the bottom step on Sunday, white as a sheet.
[SEG0009] person_1 (DOCTOR): Any chest pain when that happens?
[SEG0010] person_2 (PATIENT): No. No pain in the chest at all.
[SEG0011] person_1 (DOCTOR): And dizziness, or feeling like you'll pass out?
[SEG0012] person_2 (PATIENT): No, I wouldn't say I'm dizzy. I haven't fainted.
[SEG0013] person_1 (DOCTOR): What about your heart racing, palpitations?
[SEG0014] person_2 (PATIENT): No, nothing like that.
[SEG0015] person_1 (DOCTOR): Tell me about the periods. How many pads in a day?

[SEG0016] person_2 (PATIENT): It's been awful for my clothes, I've binned two pairs of black work trousers because of leaks, and I wear the big night pads in the daytime, the Always ones, and I still—
[SEG0017] person_1 (DOCTOR): Sorry, hold on, it's logged me out again. What was the number of pads?
[SEG0018] person_2 (PATIENT): On a bad day, six or seven, sometimes I lose count and it's more. They last eight or nine days now, they used to be about five. And I flood if I stand up too quick.
[SEG0019] person_3 (FAMILY_MEMBER): She sets an alarm in the night to change them.
[SEG0020] person_1 (DOCTOR): Clots?
[SEG0021] person_2 (PATIENT): Yes, big ones, like, I don't know, bigger than a fifty pence piece, sometimes I think the size of a pound coin but it's hard to tell when you're, well—
[SEG0022] person_1 (DOCTOR): Right, got it, clots. One second.
[SEG0023] person_1 (DOCTOR): Any chance you could be pregnant, or is there pain with the bleeding?
[SEG0024] person_2 (PATIENT): No, definitely not pregnant, my husband's had the snip. The cramps are nasty the first two days, a dragging pain low down, I take paracetamol for that.
[SEG0025] person_1 (DOCTOR): How much paracetamol?

[SEG0026] person_2 (PATIENT): Two of the five hundred milligram tablets, so a gram, when the cramps are bad, maybe twice on those days. Not the rest of the month. I don't take ibuprofen, it never agreed with my stomach years ago, so I just don't.
[SEG0027] person_3 (FAMILY_MEMBER): Can I just say, Mum's got an underactive thyroid, she's been on thyroxine for years, and Mum's sister has it too. I wondered if that's relevant.
[SEG0028] person_1 (DOCTOR): Sorry, the printer started, say that again?
[SEG0029] person_3 (FAMILY_MEMBER): Our mum, underactive thyroid, and our aunt, Mum's sister. Both of them.
[SEG0030] person_1 (DOCTOR): Thanks. Any medicines besides the paracetamol?

[SEG0031] person_2 (PATIENT): Doctor Patel said my iron was low, so ferrous sulphate, I think the dose is 200 milligrams. He said one a day, but I only take them sometimes, when I remember, some weeks every other day and then I'll skip a whole week. They make me queasy, so I put them off.
[SEG0032] person_1 (DOCTOR): So not every day. Anything else, vitamins, coil, contraceptive?

[SEG0033] person_2 (PATIENT): No coil, no pill. Just those two. Oh, and my hair, I wasn't going to mention it, but the plughole is full of it, handfuls when I wash it, and my parting looks wider, that's been a couple of months. I kept telling myself it was the cheap shampoo.
[SEG0034] person_1 (DOCTOR): Weight down at all? Clothes looser?
[SEG0035] person_2 (PATIENT): No, weight's the same, the jeans fit the same. If anything I feel bloated on my period but the scales don't move.
[SEG0036] person_1 (DOCTOR): Bowels alright? Any change there?
[SEG0037] person_2 (PATIENT): Bowels are fine, once a day, normal. No diarrhoea or anything.
[SEG0038] person_1 (DOCTOR): Any operations in the past?
[SEG0039] person_2 (PATIENT): No, never had an operation. Not even my tonsils.

[SEG0040] person_2 (PATIENT): Actually, wait, about the dizziness. I said no, but last week in the shower I went all woozy and the room went grey, and I had to sit on the edge of the bath. It happened once on the stairs as well, just a few seconds. I don't know why I said I wasn't dizzy.

[SEG0041] person_1 (DOCTOR): Okay, so there have been light-headed spells. You're pale and the conjunctivae are pale. Chest is clear and the heart sounds are normal, just a bit quick. Earlier readings were blood pressure 112 over 70, pulse 98, oxygen 98 percent.

[SEG0042] person_1 (DOCTOR): I think this is most likely iron deficiency anaemia from the heavy periods. I can't rule out an underactive thyroid, given your mum and your aunt and how tired you are, so we'll check that too.

[SEG0043] person_2 (PATIENT): Will I need a scan? My friend had fibroids and she said the scan was nothing, but I'm a bit nervous about hospitals, I had a bad time when my dad was in, not about me, sorry, I'm rambling.

[SEG0044] person_1 (DOCTOR): Blood tests first, today if the phlebotomist can fit you in. Full blood count, ferritin, and thyroid function. I'm not booking a pelvic scan now. If the bleeding stays this heavy once we've seen the bloods, then we'll arrange a pelvic ultrasound.

[SEG0045] person_1 (DOCTOR): And I want you on ferrous sulphate properly, 200 milligrams twice a day, not just when you remember. Take it with food or orange juice, and leave a gap around tea, tea blocks the absorption. If you get chest pain, or you're breathless sitting still, or you actually faint, don't wait for me, go to A&E.

[SEG0046] person_2 (PATIENT): Twice a day, with food, not with tea, and A&E if I faint or get chest pain. I can do that. Should I bring the old box so you can see the strength, because I might have the dose wrong?

[SEG0047] person_1 (DOCTOR): Yes, bring the box if you can, but start the twice daily from today anyway. Book back in with me in a fortnight for the results. Reception can sort the blood form on your way out.

spec.situation: Tired, breathless woman with heavy periods for a year; counts pads and clots in vague terms; takes iron 'sometimes'; hair loss; relative mentions thyroid in the family. Blood tests, maybe pelvic scan.
features: interruptions_trailing_off: people interrupt each other, trail off, or the answer comes two turns after the question.

denial_then_admission: the patient first denies a symptom, then later describes it. The label records the symptom as present (the later, fuller answer) and does NOT also record the earlier denial as a negative finding.
spec.doctor_style: distracted by the computer, asks for repeats

Heavy menstrual bleeding detail missing: she wakes at night / sets an alarm in the night to change pads.
Menstrual clot size detail recorded incompletely/wrongly: patient said clots were bigger than a 50 pence piece and sometimes about the size of a pound coin.

Medication intolerance/avoidance missing: she does not take ibuprofen because it upset her stomach years ago.

Weight history detail missing: weight unchanged / jeans fit the same.
Bowel history detail missing: bowels once a day and normal.

bad.reason: Most details supported; night alarm was reported by family member, not patient.
bad.text: heavy periods (category=genitourinary, status=present, duration=approximately 1 year, frequency=six or seven pads on a bad day, sometimes more; bleeding for eight or nine days, temporality=current, associated_symptoms=flooding on standing; leaking through night-time pads; sets an alarm at night to change pads, reported_by=patient, certainty=certain)

bad.reason: Patient says she does not take ibuprofen because it upset her stomach years ago; not stated as discontinued medication.

omissions.text: Negative finding recorded wrongly: dizziness was initially denied but then corrected; patient did have two recent brief light-headed/woozy episodes with greying of vision, so dizziness is not absent.
Heavy periods had worsened compared with baseline: they now last 8–9 days and used to be about 5 days.
Patient denied any change in bowels and specifically said bowels are fine, once a day, normal.
Patient is not breathless sitting still and specifically said she was not gasping while sitting there.
Reason pregnancy was considered absent: husband has had a vasectomy ('the snip').
Ibuprofen was not simply discontinued; patient avoids it because it previously upset her stomach.
Examination included mild tachycardia: heart sounds were normal but 'just a bit quick'.
Doctor said a pelvic scan was not being booked at this stage, only if bleeding remains heavy after blood results.
